SoftServe: A Scalable
Quasi-Newton Method for Deep Learning

Joohwan Ko    Tetiana Parshakova    Diana Cai Affiliation: University of Massachusetts Amherst  CCM, Flatiron Institute  Cornell University    Robert M. Gower
Abstract

Quasi-Newton (QN) methods have long been among the most effective methods for large-scale unconstrained convex optimization. Two obstacles have limited their use in deep learning: non-convexity and enormous parameter sizes. We introduce SoftServe, a family of QN methods designed to overcome these obstacles without line searches or ad hoc curvature corrections. SoftServe derives positive-definite curvature estimates from the variational objective of Berglund et al. (2025), even in the presence of negative curvature. We develop diagonal and Kronecker-factored variants that preserve positive definiteness by construction and scale to massive neural networks. Finally, SoftServe relies on the stable coupled Newton–Schulz iteration for the required matrix operations, replacing costly matrix decompositions with GPU-friendly matrix multiplications. SoftServe excels on problems that are severely ill-conditioned, including tasks such as recurrent networks, deep autoencoders, physics-informed neural networks, and a 136M-parameter physics-informed diffusion model, often achieving lower losses than established baselines including Adam, Muon, and SOAP.
22footnotetext: Work done while at the Flatiron Institute. Email: joohwanko@cs.umass.edu.33footnotetext: Equal senior authors.

1 Introduction

Quasi-Newton methods, such as the celebrated BFGS method (Broyden, 1970; Fletcher, 1970; Goldfarb, 1970; Shanno, 1970), are among the most effective methods for large-scale, convex deterministic optimization. Deep learning has led to renewed interest in adapting these methods to train large networks (Goldfarb et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2022). However, applying these methods to deep learning requires curvature estimates that can accommodate non-convex objectives and gradient noise while remaining computationally efficient.

To see how curvature enters the optimization update, consider a generic second-order method. For parameters x∈ℝDx\in\mathbb{R}^{D}, second-order methods typically take steps of the form

x+=x−γ​𝑯​g.x^{+}=x-\gamma\bm{H}g.

Here x+x^{+} is the updated parameter vector, and γ>0\gamma>0 is the step size. The vector g∈ℝDg\in\mathbb{R}^{D} is the (stochastic) gradient at xx, and the matrix 𝑯∈ℝD×D\bm{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D} is an estimate of the inverse Hessian.

Non-convexity of the objective poses a fundamental challenge for second-order optimization methods because the true Hessian could have negative eigenvalues. If the estimate 𝑯\bm{H} has a negative eigenvalue, then the update direction −𝑯​g-\bm{H}g could be an ascent direction, which would increase the loss function. This is one of the reasons why first-order methods are often preferred in deep learning: one can always guarantee descent (in expectation). For a second-order method to be applicable in deep learning, the estimate 𝑯\bm{H} must always be positive definite, even in the presence of directions of negative curvature.

For quasi-Newton methods, such as BFGS, maintaining positive definiteness is at odds with the main tool used to measure curvature, namely the secant equation. In the presence of negative curvature, enforcing the secant equation can inadvertently force the Hessian estimate to become indefinite, as we will show in Section 2. The standard remedy is to use sophisticated line search procedures to only move in directions of positive curvature (Nocedal and Wright, 2006; Wolfe, 1969). But these line searches require access to the full batch loss, which is too costly and not feasible in the stochastic setting of deep learning.

Beyond the challenges arising from non-convexity and stochastic objectives, the sheer scale of modern deep learning models makes storing and updating dense curvature estimates prohibitively expensive. A standard approach for reducing this cost is the limited memory approach of L-BFGS (Liu and Nocedal, 1989), which typically uses only 10 pairs of parameter and gradient differences to implicitly build the estimate 𝑯\bm{H}. But storing 10 pairs of parameters and gradients would require storing 10 copies of our model and 10 copies of the gradient, increasing the memory storage by 20-fold. This is infeasible for all but small models.

To scale to modern deep learning, it is common to approximate the matrix 𝑯\bm{H} by a diagonal matrix (Duchi et al., 2011; Tieleman and Hinton, 2012; Kingma and Ba, 2015) or a Kronecker-structured matrix (Martens and Grosse, 2015; Gupta et al., 2018). For quasi-Newton optimization, while Kronecker-structured updates have been proposed for applying BFGS to deep learning (Goldfarb et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2022), this approach still needs to be applied with mechanisms for handling non-convexity and stochasticity, limiting its applicability.

A promising new direction is to reconsider how curvature enters the quasi-Newton update. Recently, Berglund et al. (2025) show that by replacing the secant equation with a soft secant penalty we can ensure that our Hessian estimate is positive definite, even in the presence of negative curvature. But Berglund et al. (2025) only consider dense estimates, making their approach infeasible for deep learning.

We introduce SoftServe (Soft Secant Equation Regularized with Variational Entropy), a quasi-Newton framework that combines the flexibility of a soft secant constraint (Li, 2019; Berglund et al., 2025) with the computational advantages of a structured matrix approximation of the inverse Hessian. Optimizing within diagonal and Kronecker-structured families yields novel updates that preserve positive definiteness, without full batch evaluations or line searches. We develop efficient algorithms for computing these updates using modern GPU-friendly numerical linear algebra methods, such as variants of Newton-Schulz (Amsel et al., 2026; Higham, 2008), allowing SoftServe to scale to large neural networks.

We then demonstrate the utility of SoftServe on several deep learning tasks where curvature information is fundamental—such as severely ill-conditioned tasks—including recurrent networks, autoencoders, and physics-informed models (such as a 136M-parameter diffusion model). On these tasks we find that SoftServe often outperforms modern methods such as Adam, Muon, and SOAP. A Python implementation of SoftServe is available at https://github.com/joohwanko/SoftServe.

2 Quasi-Newton Preliminaries

Here we introduce our notation and review important quasi-Newton (QN) ideas that are relevant to SoftServe. For simplicity, in this section we represent all parameters as a flattened vector x∈ℝDx\in\mathbb{R}^{D}. We introduce the setting of deep learning in subsequent sections, where parameters can be matrices.

Notation.

We write 𝕊+⁣+d\mathbb{S}_{++}^{d} and 𝕊+d\mathbb{S}_{+}^{d} for the symmetric positive definite and positive semidefinite d×dd\times d matrices, 𝑰d\bm{I}_{d} for the identity, and we define ‖v‖𝑴2:=v⊤​𝑴​v\left\lVert v\right\rVert_{\bm{M}}^{2}:=v^{\top}\bm{M}v for 𝑴∈𝕊+⁣+d\bm{M}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{d}.

2.1 The BFGS algorithm

Let ff be a continuous, twice differentiable function on ℝD\mathbb{R}^{D}. Given iterates xtx_{t} and gradient evaluations ∇f​(xt)\nabla f(x_{t}), quasi-Newton methods use the following iterate and gradient differences

st\displaystyle s_{t} :=xt+1−xt,\displaystyle:=x_{t+1}-x_{t},
yt\displaystyle y_{t} :=∇f​(xt+1)−∇f​(xt),\displaystyle:=\nabla f(x_{t+1})-\nabla f(x_{t}),

to estimate curvature. Indeed, using Taylor’s theorem we have that

yt=𝑩t​st,y_{t}=\bm{B}_{t}s_{t}, (1)

where 𝑩t:=∫01∇2f​(xt+τ​st)​𝑑τ\bm{B}_{t}:=\int_{0}^{1}\nabla^{2}f(x_{t}+\tau s_{t})\,d\tau is the averaged Hessian. Quasi-Newton methods use Eq. 1 to find an estimate of the inverse Hessian 𝑯\bm{H} by enforcing the secant equation

\tcboxmath[equationbox,title=]𝑯yt=st.\displaystyle\tcboxmath[equationbox,title={}]{\bm{H}y_{t}=s_{t}.} (2)

However, the secant equation is underdetermined: 𝑯\bm{H} has D2D^{2} unknown entries, while Eq. 2 imposes only DD constraints. Thus, to obtain a unique update, one must impose an additional regularization criterion. Quasi-Newton methods resolve this by choosing 𝑯{\bm{H}} that both satisfies the secant equation and is close to the previous estimate 𝑯t{\bm{H}}_{t} in some sense.

For instance, the BFGS method chooses the matrix 𝑯\bm{H} that satisfies the secant equation and is closest to 𝑯t\bm{H}_{t} in a weighted Frobenius norm (Nocedal and Wright, 2006); see Appendix A.1. We adopt an equivalent characterization of the BFGS update due to Fletcher (1991), where closeness is measured by the log-determinant divergence. This formulation will be the starting point for SoftServe. For 𝑷,𝑸∈𝕊+⁣+d\bm{P},\bm{Q}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{d} the log-determinant divergence is defined as

𝒟(𝑷;𝑸):=tr(𝑷𝑸−1)−logdet(𝑷𝑸−1)−d.\mathscr{D}(\bm{P};\bm{Q}):=\operatorname{tr}(\bm{P}\bm{Q}^{-1})-\log\det(\bm{P}\bm{Q}^{-1})-d. (3)

This divergence is strictly convex in 𝑷\bm{P} (given fixed 𝑸\bm{Q}) and also is equivalent (up to a constant) to the relative entropy, or Kullback-Leibler divergence between two Gaussians with the same mean and covariances 𝑷\bm{P} and 𝑸\bm{Q}. Fletcher (1991) showed that, when st⊤​yt>0s_{t}^{\top}y_{t}>0, the BFGS update is given by the solution of the following optimization problem:

\tcboxmath[equationbox,title=]𝑯t+1BFGS=arg⁡min𝑯∈𝕊+⁣+D𝒟(𝑯t;𝑯)subject to𝑯yt=st.\displaystyle\tcboxmath[equationbox,title={}]{\bm{H}_{t+1}^{\rm BFGS}=\underset{\bm{H}\in\mathbb{S}_{\scalebox{0.7}{$\scriptscriptstyle++$}}^{D}}{\arg\min}~\mathscr{D}(\bm{H}_{t};\bm{H})\quad\text{subject to}\quad\bm{H}y_{t}=s_{t}.} (4)

What happens in the non-convex and stochastic setting?

The requirement st⊤​yt>0s_{t}^{\top}y_{t}>0 is called the curvature condition and it always holds for convex objectives, but can fail for nonconvex objectives. Indeed, if st⊤​yt<0s_{t}^{\top}y_{t}<0, then any matrix 𝑯\bm{H} satisfying the secant equation must also satisfy st⊤​yt=yt⊤​𝑯​yt<0,s_{t}^{\top}y_{t}=y_{t}^{\top}\bm{H}y_{t}<0, and thus cannot be positive definite.

In stochastic settings, the construction of the gradient difference yty_{t} requires additional care. Let ∇fξ​(x)\nabla f_{\xi}(x) denote a stochastic gradient evaluated with random draw ξ\xi, which specifies the minibatch and other sources of randomness such as data augmentation or dropout masks. In this case, we compute yt=∇fξ​(xt+1)−∇fξ​(xt)y_{t}=\nabla f_{\xi}(x_{t+1})-\nabla f_{\xi}(x_{t}) using the same draw at both endpoints, in order to ensure that the gradient difference reflects the curvature for a single sampled loss. Enforcing the secant equation Eq. 2 in the stochastic setting is also problematic, since Eq. 2 would force 𝑯{\bm{H}} to exactly fit the curvature of just one stochastic loss.

2.2 Soft quasi-Newton

Soft QN (quasi-Newton) builds on the alternative variational formulation of BFGS given in Eq. 4, relaxing the secant constraint by transforming it into a least-squares penalty in the objective function (Berglund et al., 2025). Given λ>0\lambda>0 and the current estimate 𝑯t\bm{H}_{t}, the Soft QN algorithm approximates the inverse Hessian by solving

\tcboxmath[equationbox,title=]𝑯t+1=arg⁡min𝑯∈𝕊+⁣+D‖st−𝑯yt‖𝑯−12+1λ𝒟(𝑯t;𝑯).\displaystyle\tcboxmath[equationbox,title={}]{\bm{H}_{t+1}=\underset{\bm{H}\in\mathbb{S}_{\scalebox{0.7}{$\scriptscriptstyle++$}}^{D}}{\arg\min}~\left\lVert s_{t}-\bm{H}y_{t}\right\rVert_{\bm{H}^{-1}}^{2}+\tfrac{1}{\lambda}\mathscr{D}(\bm{H}_{t};\bm{H}).} (5)

The first term in Eq. 5 penalizes the secant residual; the second term measures how far 𝑯t\bm{H}_{t} is from 𝑯\bm{H} in log-determinant divergence Eq. 3. The parameter λ>0\lambda>0 controls the tradeoff between the two terms.

Eq. 5 has several nice properties. First, it is scale invariant and strictly convex in 𝑯−1\bm{H}^{-1}. Second, there is a closed-form solution for 𝑯t+1\bm{H}_{t+1}, given in Eq. A.4. Third, the BFGS update is also a solution to Eq. 5 in the limit as λ→∞\lambda\to\infty and st⊤​yt>0s_{t}^{\top}y_{t}>0 (see Berglund et al. (2025) and Appendix A.2). Finally and crucially, Soft QN remains well-defined and positive definite for every finite pair, including those with negative curvature st⊤​yt≤0s_{t}^{\top}y_{t}\leq 0.

However, computing the solution of Eq. 5 costs 𝒪⁡(D2)\mathcal{O}(D^{2}) operations, which is computationally expensive, and the memory cost of storing the D2D^{2} matrix 𝑯\bm{H} is prohibitive in deep learning. We circumvent both the operational and memory costs by restricting to structured matrices.

3 SoftServe: Quasi-Newton Updates over Structured Families

To scale to deep neural networks, we consider two choices for structured families ℋ⊂𝕊+⁣+D\mathcal{H}\subset\mathbb{S}_{++}^{D}: a diagonal matrix family and Kronecker-structured matrix family. SoftServe then solves Eq. 5 for an inverse Hessian approximation 𝑯\bm{H} over the structured family ℋ\mathcal{H}, instead of over dense matrices in 𝕊+⁣+D\mathbb{S}_{++}^{D}. This optimization yields novel and efficiently-computable updates, which we call SoftServe-Diag and SoftServe-Kron.

Instead of the 𝒪⁡(D2)\mathcal{O}(D^{2}) cost of Soft QN, SoftServe-Diag reduces the memory and computational cost to 𝒪⁡(D)\mathcal{O}(D), which is comparable to that of Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015). SoftServe-Kron reduces the costs to 𝒪⁡(n2+m2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}+m^{2}) for each D=n×mD=n\times m parameter block, which is the cost of Shampoo (Gupta et al., 2018) and KFAC (Martens and Grosse, 2015).

3.1 Diagonal approximation

SoftServe-Diag restricts the inverse Hessian estimate 𝑯\bm{H} to be diagonal. Thus we need only store one positive scale per coordinate, 𝑯=diag⁡(h)\bm{H}=\operatorname{diag}(h) with h∈ℝ+⁣+Dh\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^{D}. Both terms of the objective in Eq. 5 then split into sums over coordinates ht+1,ih_{t+1,i}. Each coordinate is a scalar problem with a unique, closed-form solution ht+1,i>0h_{t+1,i}>0 (Lemma B.1), given by

\tcboxmath[equationbox,title=]ht+1,i=2​(ht,i+λ​st,i2)1+1+4​λ​yt,i2​(ht,i+λ​st,i2),i=1,…,D.\displaystyle\tcboxmath[equationbox,title={}]{h_{t+1,i}=\frac{2\left(h_{t,i}+\lambda s_{t,i}^{2}\right)}{1+\sqrt{1+4\lambda y_{t,i}^{2}\left(h_{t,i}+\lambda s_{t,i}^{2}\right)}},\qquad i=1,\ldots,D.} (6)

Thus, the matrix estimate is 𝑯t+1=diag⁡(ht+1)\bm{H}_{t+1}=\operatorname{diag}(h_{t+1}). Though SoftServe-Diag is inexpensive, and can perform reasonably well, it ignores all interactions between coordinates.

3.2 Kronecker-structured approximation

Neural network parameters are often naturally represented as matrices. Let 𝑿∈ℝn×m\bm{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} denote a layer’s weight matrix and 𝑮:=∇𝑿f∈ℝn×m\bm{G}:=\nabla_{\bm{X}}f\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} denote its gradient. Thus the Hessian matrix associated with 𝑿\bm{X} has n2​m2n^{2}m^{2} entries. We can reduce this storage cost by imposing a Kronecker structure:

\tcboxmath[equationbox,title=]𝑯=𝑳⊗𝑹,where𝑳∈𝕊+⁣+m,𝑹∈𝕊+⁣+n.\tcboxmath[equationbox,title={}]{\bm{H}=\bm{L}\otimes\bm{R},\quad\mbox{where}\quad\bm{L}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{m},\quad\bm{R}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{n}.} (7)

Here ⊗\otimes denotes the Kronecker product: if 𝑳=[ai​j]\bm{L}=[a_{ij}], then 𝑳⊗𝑹\bm{L}\otimes\bm{R} is the n​m×n​mnm\times nm block matrix whose (i,j)th(i,j)^{\text{th}} block is ai​j​𝑹a_{ij}\bm{R}. Storing the two factors 𝑳\bm{L} and 𝑹\bm{R} requires only m2+n2m^{2}+n^{2} entries. By Eq. B.4, applying 𝑯\bm{H} to the gradient also requires only two matrix products: 𝑯​g=vec⁡(𝑹​𝑮​𝑳),\bm{H}g=\operatorname{vec}(\bm{R}\bm{G}\bm{L}), where g=vec⁡(𝑮)g=\operatorname{vec}(\bm{G}) and vec⁡(⋅)\operatorname{vec}(\cdot) stacks columns.

Unfortunately there is no closed-form solution when minimizing the soft quasi-Newton objective Eq. 5 over both 𝑳\bm{L} and 𝑹\bm{R}. But there is a unique solution if we solve for only one factor at a time. We therefore update them alternately, holding one fixed while optimizing the other. As we now show, each conditional minimization reduces to solving a quadratic matrix equation with a unique positive-definite solution (see Lemma B.3).

To see this, we first reshape the secant vectors into matrices 𝑺t,𝒀t∈ℝn×m\bm{S}_{t},\bm{Y}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}, with vec⁡(𝑺t)=st\operatorname{vec}(\bm{S}_{t})=s_{t} and vec⁡(𝒀t)=yt.\operatorname{vec}(\bm{Y}_{t})=y_{t}. Holding 𝑹=𝑹t\bm{R}=\bm{R}_{t} fixed and minimizing the terms in Eq. 5 involving 𝑳\bm{L}, we obtain the conditional update

\tcboxmath[equationbox,title=]𝑳t+1=arg​min𝐋∈𝕊+⁣+mtr(𝐔L𝐋)+tr(𝐕L𝐋−1)+logdet𝐋,\displaystyle\tcboxmath[equationbox,title={}]{\bm{L}_{t+1}=\argmin_{\bm{L}\in\mathbb{S}_{\scalebox{0.7}{$\scriptscriptstyle++$}}^{m}}\quad\operatorname{tr}(\bm{U}_{L}\bm{L})+\operatorname{tr}(\bm{V}_{L}\bm{L}^{-1})+\log\det\bm{L},} (8)

where we define the auxiliary matrices:

𝑼L:=λn​𝒀t⊤​𝑹t​𝒀tand𝑽L:=𝑳t+λn​𝑺t⊤​𝑹t−1​𝑺t.\bm{U}_{L}:=\tfrac{\lambda}{n}\bm{Y}_{t}^{\top}\bm{R}_{t}\bm{Y}_{t}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\bm{V}_{L}:=\bm{L}_{t}+\tfrac{\lambda}{n}\bm{S}_{t}^{\top}\bm{R}_{t}^{-1}\bm{S}_{t}. (9)

Differentiating Eq. 8 with respect to 𝑳\bm{L} and setting the derivative to zero, yields the quadratic matrix equation

\tcboxmath[equationbox,title=]𝑳𝑼L𝑳+𝑳=𝑽L.\displaystyle\tcboxmath[equationbox,title={}]{\bm{L}\,\bm{U}_{L}\,\bm{L}+\bm{L}=\bm{V}_{L}.} (10)

Here, because 𝑼L⪰0\bm{U}_{L}\succeq 0 and 𝑽L≻0\bm{V}_{L}\succ 0, this equation has a unique, positive-definite solution 𝑳t+1\bm{L}_{t+1}, which we provide in Eq. 13 and discuss further in Section 4.1.

We then update the factor 𝑹\bm{R} by minimizing Eq. 5 in 𝑹\bm{R} and holding 𝑳t+1\bm{L}_{t+1} fixed:

\tcboxmath[equationbox,title=]𝑹t+1=arg​min𝐑∈𝕊+⁣+ntr(𝐔R𝐑)+tr(𝐕R𝐑−1)+logdet𝐑,\displaystyle\tcboxmath[equationbox,title={}]{\bm{R}_{t+1}=\argmin_{\bm{R}\in\mathbb{S}_{\scalebox{0.7}{$\scriptscriptstyle++$}}^{n}}\quad\operatorname{tr}(\bm{U}_{R}\bm{R})+\operatorname{tr}(\bm{V}_{R}\bm{R}^{-1})+\log\det\bm{R},} (11)

where the auxiliary matrices are now defined as

𝑼R:=λm​𝒀t​𝑳t+1​𝒀t⊤and𝑽R:=m−1​[tr⁡(𝑳t​𝑳t+1−1)​𝑹t+λ​𝑺t​𝑳t+1−1​𝑺t⊤].\bm{U}_{R}:=\tfrac{\lambda}{m}\bm{Y}_{t}\bm{L}_{t+1}\bm{Y}_{t}^{\top}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\bm{V}_{R}:=m^{-1}[\operatorname{tr}(\bm{L}_{t}\bm{L}_{t+1}^{-1})\bm{R}_{t}+\lambda\bm{S}_{t}\bm{L}_{t+1}^{-1}\bm{S}_{t}^{\top}]. (12)

Solving Eq. 11 for 𝑹t+1\bm{R}_{t+1} reduces to solving an analogous quadratic matrix equation to Eq. 10, 𝑹​𝑼R​𝑹+𝑹=𝑽R\bm{R}\,\bm{U}_{R}\,\bm{R}+\bm{R}=\bm{V}_{R}, which again has a unique, positive-definite solution (Lemma B.3).

The alternating updates replace computations on the full inverse-Hessian estimate 𝑯\bm{H} with operations on the two smaller factors 𝑳\bm{L} and 𝑹\bm{R}. Nevertheless, directly solving the quadratic matrix equations can be expensive for wide layers, with cost 𝒪⁡(n3+m3+n2​m+n​m2)\mathcal{O}(n^{3}+m^{3}+n^{2}m+nm^{2}). Instead of using a direct solver, we will use GPU-friendly Newton-Schulz approximations, as discussed in the next section. Using Newton-Schulz approximations was also central to Muon’s effectiveness at scale (Amsel et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025).

4 Practical implementation of SoftServe for deep learning

Here we discuss strategies to make SoftServe practical for training deep neural networks.

4.1 Efficient Kronecker updates

SoftServe-Kron requires solving quadratic matrix equations (Cai et al., 2024), which are particular instances of the algebraic Riccati equation (Lancaster and Rodman, 1995). Here we discuss how to approximately solve this matrix equation using a GPU friendly approach. These approximations are key for scaling SoftServe up to large neural networks.

Both Kronecker factor updates in Eq. 8 and Eq. 11 reduce to solving a quadratic matrix equation of the form 𝑸​𝑼​𝑸+𝑸=𝑽\bm{Q}\bm{U}\bm{Q}+\bm{Q}=\bm{V} with 𝑼⪰0\bm{U}\succeq 0 and 𝑽≻0\bm{V}\succ 0. Its unique positive-definite solution can be expressed using principal matrix square roots 𝑽1/2\bm{V}^{1/2} (see Appendix B.3):

\tcboxmath[equationbox,title=]𝑸=2𝑽1/2[𝑰d+(𝑰d+4𝑽1/2𝑼𝑽1/2)1/2]−1𝑽1/2.\tcboxmath[equationbox,title={}]{\bm{Q}=2\bm{V}^{1/2}\left[\bm{I}_{d}+\left(\bm{I}_{d}+4\bm{V}^{1/2}\bm{U}\bm{V}^{1/2}\right)^{1/2}\right]^{-1}\bm{V}^{1/2}.} (13)

Direct evaluation of Eq. 13 requires two matrix square roots and a matrix inverse. For Kronecker updates, the coefficients admit a natural Gram matrix factorization 𝑼=𝑭​𝑭⊤\bm{U}=\bm{F}\bm{F}^{\top}, given in Section C.1. Our implementation exploits this structure through an equivalent Gram formulation of Eq. 13 given in Eq. B.22, which evaluates a square root of 𝑰+4​𝑭⊤​𝑽​𝑭\bm{I}+4\bm{F}^{\top}\bm{V}\bm{F} and an inverse, which avoids the separate square roots of 𝑽\bm{V}. See Appendix B.3 and C.1 for details.

While the matrix functions in Eq. 13 can be computed using, for instance singular value decomposition (SVD), most methods for computing the SVD are not well suited for GPUs (Heavner et al., 2023). To compute the matrix square root efficiently on GPUs, we use the coupled Newton-Schulz iteration (Higham, 1997; Higham, 2008), which is based only on matrix multiplications and additions. For a positive definite matrix 𝑴\bm{M}, coupled Newton-Schulz jointly approximates its square root 𝑴12\bm{M}^{\frac{1}{2}} and its inverse square root 𝑴−12\bm{M}^{-\frac{1}{2}}. Matrix inverses are likewise approximated using Newton-Schulz iterations. See Appendix C.2 for details.

4.2 Training with SoftServe

To make SoftServe practical, we make use of several now-standard practices in deep learning. The full procedure includes momentum updates, Nesterov extrapolation or bias correction (Kingma and Ba, 2015), details of which are in Appendix D.1.

Algorithm 1 summarizes one training iteration of SoftServe-Kron applied to one matrix parameter 𝑿∈ℝn×m.{\bm{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}. SoftServe-Diag follows the same procedure replacing the Kronecker updates with the diagonal update in Eq. 6, and detailed in Algorithm D.2

One of main changes we have introduced in Algorithm 1 is that we use a normalized update, see line 2. In vectorized notation, this normalized update is given by

xt+1=xt−γt​𝑯t​m^t/m^t⊤​𝑯t​m^t,\displaystyle x_{t+1}=x_{t}-\gamma_{t}\bm{H}_{t}\hat{m}_{t}\,\Big/\sqrt{\hat{m}_{t}^{\top}\bm{H}_{t}\hat{m}_{t}}, (14)

where xt=vec⁡(𝑿t),m^t=vec⁡(𝑴^t)x_{t}=\operatorname{vec}(\bm{X}_{t}),\hat{m}_{t}=\operatorname{vec}(\hat{\bm{M}}_{t}) and 𝑯t=𝑳t⊗𝑹t.\bm{H}_{t}=\bm{L}_{t}\otimes\bm{R}_{t}. By Eqs. B.4 and B.5, Eq. 14 is equivalent to the matrix update on line 2 of Algorithm 1. Normalized updates are often more effective in deep learning (Jordan et al., 2024; Pethick et al., 2025; Crawshaw et al., 2026), which we also confirmed in our initial experiments.

Finally, to amortize the cost of refreshing the curvature estimate, we hold 𝑯t\bm{H}_{t} fixed for KK training steps. At the beginning of each window, we save the parameters, stochastic gradient, and random draw. At the end, we reevaluate the gradient using the saved draw, forming a secant pair from the endpoint differences, see Appendix D.1 for details.

5 Related Work

Stochastic and structured Quasi-Newton.

Classical QN methods enforce the secant equation while changing the metric as little as possible (Broyden, 1970; Fletcher, 1970; Goldfarb, 1970; Shanno, 1970; Dennis and Moré, 1977; Nocedal and Wright, 2006). Stochastic variants keep a dense or limited-memory metric (Liu and Nocedal, 1989) and protect it from bad pairs by: using damping (Schraudolph et al., 2007), curvature pairs from Hessian-vector products on large batches (Byrd et al., 2016), damped updates  (Wang et al., 2017), overlapping batches (Berahas et al., 2016), diagonal rescaling (Bordes et al., 2009), or a secant penalty (Irwin and Haber, 2023). K-BFGS (Goldfarb et al., 2020) uses a per-layer Kronecker factorization of BFGS, and relies on damping for a resulting positive definite curvature estimate.

Matrix-aware methods.

There are now a growing number of methods which are specialized to the matrix parameters in linear layers. K-FAC (Martens and Grosse, 2015), Shampoo (Gupta et al., 2018), and SOAP (Vyas et al., 2025) all make use of Kronecker factorizations to form a preconditioner. Muon (Jordan et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025) is a steepest descent method in the matrix spectral norm.

Related variational objectives.

With the mean held fixed, the covariance subproblem in batch-and-match variational inference (Cai et al., 2024) has the same form as the soft QN objective in Eq. 5, which is where the closed form in Eq. 13 originates (see Section A.3 for details). The least squares secant penalty within the soft QN objective (Eq. 5) has also been used to design preconditioned variants of SGD called PSGD in (Li, 2018; Pooladzandi and Li, 2024). PSGD then uses a form of multiplicative SGD applied to the secant penalty to estimate the preconditioner.

6 Experiments

We evaluate SoftServe on recurrent sequence learning, image reconstruction, and physics-informed learning, from a small recurrent network to a 136M-parameter diffusion model. We test whether the structured inverse Hessian estimates improve training over first-order and other preconditioned methods. We compare training losses at equal gradient-evaluation budgets, and report prediction errors and wall-clock comparisons in Appendix E.

Comparison protocol.

Our baselines are Adam, Muon, SOAP, K-FAC, and K-BFGS(L), with L-BFGS also included for deterministic training. To assess the contribution of the learned inverse Hessian, we include SoftServe-I: the normalized momentum method Eq. 14 obtained by fixing 𝑯=𝑰\bm{H}=\bm{I}. We tune each method’s learning rate separately and evaluate the selected configurations on three fresh seeds. All SoftServe runs refresh the inverse Hessian estimate every K=10K=10 updates. Gradient counts include the additional evaluations used for secant pairs, line searches, and loss balancing. In stochastic training, SoftServe uses one extra gradient evaluation every KK updates to form a secant pair on the same batch, see detailed pseudo-code in Algorithm D.1. Task-specific settings and learning-rate sweeps are given in Appendix E.

6.1 RNN Adding

The Adding problem tests a recurrent network’s ability to retain information over a long sequence. Each input contains 100 numbers sampled uniformly from [0,1][0,1] and markers identifying two positions. The network reads the full sequence and predicts the sum of the two marked numbers. We train a tanh RNN with 16 hidden units by minimizing mean squared error (MSE) on batches of 128 newly sampled sequences. Although the network is small, repeated applications of the recurrent map can cause gradients to vanish or explode (Pascanu et al., 2013). The full loss Hessian in this example is numerically nearly singular at initialization across four seeds (Appendix E.2). This makes Adding an interesting ill-conditioned small-scale test. Indeed, in Figure 1 we see that preconditioning was necessary to reach a reasonable loss, with SoftServe-Kron reaching by far the lowest training loss (Figure 1, left), outperforming our baselines on all three seeds. SoftServe-Kron mean test MSE is 6.6×10−66.6\times 10^{-6}, compared with 1.5×10−41.5\times 10^{-4} for Muon and 1.0×10−21.0\times 10^{-2} for SoftServe-I.

6.2 MNIST autoencoder

We next consider MNIST reconstruction, a standard benchmark for second-order optimization (Hinton and Salakhutdinov, 2006; Martens, 2010; Goldfarb et al., 2020). A 2.8M-parameter feed-forward autoencoder compresses each 28×2828\times 28 image into a 30-dimensional representation and reconstructs the input. We minimize pixelwise binary cross-entropy with ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization, using either all 60,000 training images at each update or minibatches of 1,000. These two settings compare deterministic and stochastic training of the same network.

SoftServe-Kron reaches the lowest training objective with full batches and is close to Muon with minibatches (Figure 1, middle, right). It improves on SoftServe-I in both settings. Appendix E.3 shows held-out reconstruction errors and wall-clock comparisons.

6.3 Physics-informed neural networks

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) approximate solutions to partial differential equations (PDEs) by mapping space–time coordinates to solution values. They are trained by penalizing the PDE residual and errors in the initial and boundary conditions. Depending on the differential operator, this loss can be very ill-conditioned, motivating the use of second-order optimization (Rathore et al., 2024). We evaluate SoftServe on both small feed-forward PINNs and the larger residual architecture PirateNet (Wang et al., 2024).

Small PINNs.

We use the Wave, Convection, and Reaction problems of Rathore et al. (2024). Each network has three hidden layers of width 200 and 81,201 parameters. Training minimizes the sum of the mean squared residuals of the governing PDE and its associated initial and boundary conditions. We either fix the sampled training coordinates (collocation points) or resample them at each update. This gives six settings across the three equations.

SoftServe-Kron attains the lowest final training objective in five of the six settings, including all three with resampled points (Figure 2). On deterministic Wave, Adam and Adam+L-BFGS attain lower final losses, with Adam+L-BFGS achieving the lowest. Adam+L-BFGS, used by Rathore et al. (2024), runs Adam for the first 11,000 parameter updates, followed by L-BFGS within the remaining gradient-evaluation budget. Appendix E.4 gives solution errors and repeats the comparison in double precision.

For our remaining experiments with larger models below, we restrict the baselines to Adam, Muon, and SOAP, based on their scalability, and performance in the preceding experiments.

PirateNet.

PirateNet is a PINN architecture that combines fully connected layers with skip connections to make deeper networks easier to train. We use a 0.73M-parameter model to solve the Allen–Cahn and Korteweg–de Vries (KdV) equations. Training uses 32,768 collocation points per update and adaptive weights for the loss terms. Since these weights differ across optimizers, we compare the unweighted sum of PDE and initial-condition MSE on the same fixed points. Against Adam, Muon, and SOAP, SoftServe-Kron is competitive with Muon on Allen–Cahn and reaches the lowest mean loss on KdV (Figure 3, left and middle). The PDEs and solution errors are given in Appendix E.5.

6.4 Physics-informed diffusion

To test SoftServe at a larger scale, we train the physics-informed diffusion model (PIDM) of Bastek et al. (2025) for structural design. Given applied forces, supports, and a material budget, the model learns to place material on a two-dimensional grid to form a stiff structure. We use the 136M-parameter U-Net and 30,000 optimized training structures. The network reconstructs material-density and displacement fields from noisy inputs. Its objective combines denoising error with penalties for force imbalance, material-volume error, and compliance, a measure of structural flexibility. At 100,000 gradient evaluations, SoftServe-Kron reaches a lower mean training loss than Adam, Muon, and SOAP (Figure 3, right).

6.5 Language model

Finally, we evaluate a 16M-parameter GPT-style language model (Radford et al., 2019). It has four layers, four attention heads per layer, hidden width 256, and a context length of 512 tokens. We minimize next-token cross-entropy on 200M tokens from FineWeb (Penedo et al., 2024). SoftServe-Kron reaches a mean validation NLL of 4.6614.661, lower than AdamW (4.7864.786) but higher than Muon (4.4404.440) and SOAP (4.4164.416). Thus, the gains on the preceding tasks do not extend to matching Muon and SOAP on this language model.

7 Discussion and Limitations

We introduce SoftServe, a quasi-Newton approach for deep learning. SoftServe considers structured Hessian approximations that are always positive definite, GPU-friendly Newton–Schulz approximations, allowing it to scale to massive neural networks. Our experiments highlight the value of curvature on several ill-conditioned tasks, including recurrent networks, autoencoders, and physics-informed models, including the 136M-parameter PIDM.

Many future directions remain. For instance, currently we use a fixed λ\lambda within each training run. Developing adaptive λ\lambda would further optimize performance. Finally, characterizing convergence guarantees under realistic settings remains an open problem to study.
