Appendix contents

Appendix A BFGS and Soft quasi-Newton

A.1 BFGS

Typically, the BFGS update is derived via a weighted Frobenius norm objective that seeks to find the closest symmetric matrix to the current iterate’s quasi-Newton matrix such that the secant equation is satisfied (Nocedal and Wright, 2006, Chapter 6). That is,

𝑯t+1=arg​min𝐇∈𝕊+⁣+⁡‖𝐇−𝐇t‖F⁡(𝐖) subject to 𝐇=𝐇⊤,𝐇​yt=st,\displaystyle\bm{H}_{t+1}=\argmin_{\bm{H}\in\mathbb{S}_{\scalebox{0.7}{$\scriptscriptstyle++$}}}\|\bm{H}-\bm{H}_{t}\|_{F(\bm{W})}\quad\text{~subject~to~}\quad\bm{H}=\bm{H}^{\top},\quad\bm{H}y_{t}=s_{t}, (A.1)

where the norm above is the weighted Frobenius norm ‖𝑴‖F⁡(𝑾)=‖𝑾12​𝑴​𝑾12‖F\|\bm{M}\|_{F(\bm{W})}=\left\lVert\bm{W}^{\frac{1}{2}}\bm{M}\bm{W}^{\frac{1}{2}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}} with a weighting matrix 𝑾\bm{W} that satisfies the secant equation (e.g., 𝑾=𝑩t\bm{W}=\bm{B}_{t}).

The BFGS update is given by

\tcboxmath[equationbox,title=]𝑯t+1BFGS=(𝑰−st​yt⊤yt⊤​st)𝑯t(𝑰−yt​st⊤yt⊤​st)+st​st⊤yt⊤​st.\displaystyle\tcboxmath[equationbox,title={}]{\bm{H}_{t+1}^{\text{BFGS}}=\left(\bm{I}-\frac{s_{t}y_{t}^{\top}}{y_{t}^{\top}s_{t}}\right)\bm{H}_{t}\left(\bm{I}-\frac{y_{t}s_{t}^{\top}}{y_{t}^{\top}s_{t}}\right)+\frac{s_{t}s_{t}^{\top}}{y_{t}^{\top}s_{t}}.} (A.2)

The log-determinant formulation of Fletcher (1991) given in Eq. 4 recovers the same update, providing the starting point for replacing the secant equation with a soft penalty.

A.2 Soft quasi-Newton

As discussed in the main text, Soft QN (Berglund et al., 2025) then considers the soft penalty, regularized by the log-determinant divergence: the Soft QN algorithm then approximates the inverse Hessian by solving

𝑯t+1=arg⁡min𝑯∈𝕊+⁣+D​‖st−𝑯​yt‖𝑯−12+1λ​𝒟​(𝑯t,𝑯).\displaystyle\bm{H}_{t+1}=\underset{\bm{H}\in\mathbb{S}_{\scalebox{0.7}{$\scriptscriptstyle++$}}^{D}}{\arg\min}~\left\lVert s_{t}-\bm{H}y_{t}\right\rVert_{\bm{H}^{-1}}^{2}+\tfrac{1}{\lambda}\mathscr{D}(\bm{H}_{t};\bm{H}). (A.3)

Berglund et al. (2025) show that this objective has the unique, positive definite solution

\tcboxmath[equationbox,title=]𝑯t+1=𝑽t−4​λ​𝑽t​yt​yt⊤​𝑽t(1+1+4​λ​yt⊤​𝑽t​yt)2,\tcboxmath[equationbox,title={}]{\bm{H}_{t+1}=\bm{V}_{t}-\frac{4\lambda\bm{V}_{t}\,y_{t}y_{t}^{\top}\,\bm{V}_{t}}{\big(1+\sqrt{1+4\lambda y_{t}^{\top}\bm{V}_{t}y_{t}}\big)^{2}},} (A.4)

where 𝑽t:=𝑯t+λ​st​st⊤\bm{V}_{t}:=\bm{H}_{t}+\lambda s_{t}s_{t}^{\top}. Furthermore, Berglund et al. (2025, Theorem 3.2) shows that the BFGS update is recovered as a limiting case: under positive curvature st⊤​yt>0s_{t}^{\top}y_{t}>0, then

\tcboxmath[equationbox,title=]𝑯t+1→𝑯t+1BFGS,asλ→∞.\displaystyle\tcboxmath[equationbox,title={}]{\bm{H}_{t+1}\to\bm{H}_{t+1}^{\rm BFGS},\qquad\text{as}\quad\lambda\to\infty.} (A.5)

A.3 Connections with Variational inference

For Gaussians with a common mean μ\mu, the log-determinant divergence defined in Eq. 3 equals twice the KL divergence, that is

𝒟(𝑷;𝑸)=2KL(𝒩(μ,𝑷)∥𝒩(μ,𝑸)).\mathscr{D}(\bm{P};\bm{Q})=2\,\mathrm{KL}(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\bm{P})\,\|\,\mathcal{N}(\mu,\bm{Q})).

Let π=𝒩⁡(μ,𝑯)\pi=\mathcal{N}(\mu,\bm{H}), πt=𝒩⁡(μ,𝑯t)\pi_{t}=\mathcal{N}(\mu,\bm{H}_{t}), and let pp be a differentiable positive density. With s=μ−zs=\mu-z and y=∇z​log​p​(z)y=\nabla_{z}\log p(z), the Gaussian score is ∇z​log​π​(z)=𝑯−1​s\nabla_{z}\log\pi(z)=\bm{H}^{-1}s, so

‖∇zlogπ(z)−y‖𝑯2=‖s−𝑯y‖𝑯−12,2λKL(πt∥π)=1λ𝒟(𝑯t;𝑯).\left\lVert\nabla_{z}\log\pi(z)-y\right\rVert_{\bm{H}}^{2}=\left\lVert s-\bm{H}y\right\rVert_{\bm{H}^{-1}}^{2},\qquad\tfrac{2}{\lambda}\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{t}\|\pi)=\tfrac{1}{\lambda}\mathscr{D}(\bm{H}_{t};\bm{H}). (A.6)

Thus, the objective in  Eq. A.3 is the one-score covariance objective of Cai et al. (2024) with the mean fixed. The identity links the two covariance subproblems; it does not equate variational inference with quasi-Newton optimization.

Appendix B SoftServe: structured updates

Recall that SoftServe solves the soft quasi-Newton objective with respect to a structured matrix family ℋ\mathcal{H} (diagonal or Kronecker factored):

\tcboxmath[equationbox,title=]𝑯t+1=arg⁡min𝑯∈ℋ‖st−𝑯yt‖𝑯−12+1λ𝒟(𝑯t;𝑯).\displaystyle\tcboxmath[equationbox,title={}]{\bm{H}_{t+1}=\underset{\bm{H}\in\mathcal{H}}{\arg\min}~\left\lVert s_{t}-\bm{H}y_{t}\right\rVert_{\bm{H}^{-1}}^{2}+\tfrac{1}{\lambda}\mathscr{D}(\bm{H}_{t};\bm{H}).} (B.1)

B.1 Diagonal update

We begin by considering the diagonal family

ℋDiag\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\rm Diag} ={diag⁡(h):h∈ℝ+⁣+D}.\displaystyle=\{\operatorname{diag}(h):h\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^{D}\}.

The lemma below derives the update.

B.1Exact diagonal update.

Let ht∈ℝ+⁣+Dh_{t}\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^{D}, 𝑯t=diag⁡(ht)\bm{H}_{t}=\operatorname{diag}(h_{t}), st,yt∈ℝDs_{t},y_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}, and λ>0\lambda>0. The diagonal restriction of Eq. B.1 has the unique minimizer 𝑯t+1=diag⁡(ht+1)\bm{H}_{t+1}=\operatorname{diag}(h_{t+1}), where

ht+1,i=2​(ht,i+λ​st,i2)1+1+4​λ​yt,i2​(ht,i+λ​st,i2),i=1,…,D.h_{t+1,i}=\frac{2\left(h_{t,i}+\lambda s_{t,i}^{2}\right)}{1+\sqrt{1+4\lambda y_{t,i}^{2}\left(h_{t,i}+\lambda s_{t,i}^{2}\right)}},\qquad i=1,\ldots,D. (B.2)

Hence ht+1∈ℝ+⁣+Dh_{t+1}\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^{D}, regardless of the signs of st,i​yt,is_{t,i}y_{t,i}.

Proof.

For 𝑯=diag⁡(h)\bm{H}=\operatorname{diag}(h), the terms of Eq. B.1 that depend on hh are

∑i=1D[st,i2hi+hi​yt,i2+1λ​(ht,ihi+log⁡hi)].\sum_{i=1}^{D}\left[\frac{s_{t,i}^{2}}{h_{i}}+h_{i}y_{t,i}^{2}+\frac{1}{\lambda}\left(\frac{h_{t,i}}{h_{i}}+\log h_{i}\right)\right].

Fix ii, set v=ht,i+λ​st,i2>0v=h_{t,i}+\lambda s_{t,i}^{2}>0 and b=hi−1b=h_{i}^{-1}, and multiply by λ\lambda. The scalar problem is

minimizeb>0ψ⁡(b),ψ⁡(b)=v​b+λ​yt,i2b−log⁡b.\begin{array}[]{cc}\underset{b>0}{\mbox{minimize}}&\psi(b),\qquad\psi(b)=vb+\frac{\lambda y_{t,i}^{2}}{b}-\log b.\end{array}

Since ψ′′​(b)=2​λ​yt,i2/b3+1/b2>0\psi^{\prime\prime}(b)=2\lambda y_{t,i}^{2}/b^{3}+1/b^{2}>0 and ψ⁡(b)→+∞\psi(b)\to+\infty as b↓0b\downarrow 0 or b→∞b\to\infty, the minimizer exists and is unique. The stationarity condition λ​yt,i2​hi2+hi−v=0\lambda y_{t,i}^{2}h_{i}^{2}+h_{i}-v=0 has the single positive root

hi=2​v1+1+4​λ​yt,i2​v,h_{i}=\frac{2v}{1+\sqrt{1+4\lambda y_{t,i}^{2}v}},

which also covers yt,i=0y_{t,i}=0. Separability over ii proves the claim. ∎

B.2 Kronecker update

We state standard identities for Kronecker products (Horn and Johnson, 2012).

B.2.

For 𝑷∈ℝm×m\bm{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}, 𝑸∈ℝn×n\bm{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, and conformable 𝑿,𝒁\bm{X},\bm{Z}, we have:

(𝑷1⊗𝑸1)​(𝑷2⊗𝑸2)\displaystyle(\bm{P}_{1}\otimes\bm{Q}_{1})(\bm{P}_{2}\otimes\bm{Q}_{2}) =(𝑷1​𝑷2)⊗(𝑸1​𝑸2)\displaystyle=(\bm{P}_{1}\bm{P}_{2})\otimes(\bm{Q}_{1}\bm{Q}_{2}) (B.3)
(𝑷⊗𝑸)​vec⁡(𝑿)\displaystyle(\bm{P}\otimes\bm{Q})\operatorname{vec}(\bm{X}) =vec⁡(𝑸​𝑿​𝑷⊤)\displaystyle=\operatorname{vec}(\bm{Q}\bm{X}\bm{P}^{\top}) (B.4)
vec⁡(𝑿)⊤​vec⁡(𝒁)\displaystyle\operatorname{vec}(\bm{X})^{\top}\operatorname{vec}(\bm{Z}) =tr⁡(𝑿⊤​𝒁)\displaystyle=\operatorname{tr}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{Z}) (B.5)
tr⁡(𝑷⊗𝑸)\displaystyle\operatorname{tr}(\bm{P}\otimes\bm{Q}) =tr⁡(𝑷)​tr⁡(𝑸)\displaystyle=\operatorname{tr}(\bm{P})\operatorname{tr}(\bm{Q}) (B.6)
det(𝑷⊗𝑸)\displaystyle\det(\bm{P}\otimes\bm{Q}) =det(𝑷)n​det(𝑸)m.\displaystyle=\det(\bm{P})^{n}\det(\bm{Q})^{m}. (B.7)

We now consider the Kronecker-structured family:

ℋKron\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\rm Kron} ={𝑳⊗𝑹:𝑳∈𝕊+⁣+m,𝑹∈𝕊+⁣+n}.\displaystyle=\{\bm{L}\otimes\bm{R}:\bm{L}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{m},\bm{R}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{n}\}. (B.8)

Here, we derive the alternating update from Section 3.2. First, we recall some notation. Write st=vec⁡(𝑺t)s_{t}=\operatorname{vec}(\bm{S}_{t}), yt=vec⁡(𝒀t)y_{t}=\operatorname{vec}(\bm{Y}_{t}), and 𝑯t=𝑳t⊗𝑹t\bm{H}_{t}=\bm{L}_{t}\otimes\bm{R}_{t}. The following result establishes the properties of these conditional updates.

B.3Alternating Kronecker solution..

Let 𝑳t∈𝕊+⁣+m\bm{L}_{t}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{m}, 𝑹t∈𝕊+⁣+n\bm{R}_{t}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{n}, λ>0\lambda>0, and 𝑺t,𝒀t∈ℝn×m\bm{S}_{t},\bm{Y}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}. Consider the objective given in Eq. 5 and the updates

𝑳t+1\displaystyle\bm{L}_{t+1} =arg​min𝐋∈𝕊+⁣+mtr(𝐔L𝐋)+tr(𝐕L𝐋−1)+logdet𝐋\displaystyle=\argmin_{\bm{L}\in\mathbb{S}_{\scalebox{0.7}{$\scriptscriptstyle++$}}^{m}}\quad\operatorname{tr}(\bm{U}_{L}\bm{L})+\operatorname{tr}(\bm{V}_{L}\bm{L}^{-1})+\log\det\bm{L} (B.9)
𝑹t+1\displaystyle\bm{R}_{t+1} =arg​min𝐑∈𝕊+⁣+ntr(𝐔R𝐑)+tr(𝐕R𝐑−1)+logdet𝐑,\displaystyle=\argmin_{\bm{R}\in\mathbb{S}_{\scalebox{0.7}{$\scriptscriptstyle++$}}^{n}}\quad\operatorname{tr}(\bm{U}_{R}\bm{R})+\operatorname{tr}(\bm{V}_{R}\bm{R}^{-1})+\log\det\bm{R}, (B.10)

where we define the auxiliary matrices:

𝑼L\displaystyle\bm{U}_{L} :=λn𝒀t⊤𝑹t𝒀t and𝑽L:=𝑳t+λn𝑺t⊤𝑹t−1𝑺t\displaystyle:=\tfrac{\lambda}{n}\bm{Y}_{t}^{\top}\bm{R}_{t}\bm{Y}_{t}\quad\mbox{~~and}\quad\bm{V}_{L}:=\bm{L}_{t}+\tfrac{\lambda}{n}\bm{S}_{t}^{\top}\bm{R}_{t}^{-1}\bm{S}_{t} (B.11)
𝑼R\displaystyle\bm{U}_{R} :=λm𝒀t𝑳t+1𝒀t⊤and𝑽R:=m−1[tr(𝑳t𝑳t+1−1)𝑹t+λ𝑺t𝑳t+1−1𝑺t⊤].\displaystyle:=\tfrac{\lambda}{m}\bm{Y}_{t}\bm{L}_{t+1}\bm{Y}_{t}^{\top}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\bm{V}_{R}:=m^{-1}[\operatorname{tr}(\bm{L}_{t}\bm{L}_{t+1}^{-1})\bm{R}_{t}+\lambda\bm{S}_{t}\bm{L}_{t+1}^{-1}\bm{S}_{t}^{\top}]. (B.12)

These updates have a unique, closed-form solution that costs 𝒪⁡(n3+m3+n2​m+n​m2)\mathcal{O}(n^{3}+m^{3}+n^{2}m+nm^{2}) to compute exactly. Furthermore, the updates to 𝑳\bm{L} and 𝑹\bm{R} monotonically decrease the soft QN objective.

Proof.

Substituting 𝑯=𝑳⊗𝑹\bm{H}=\bm{L}\otimes\bm{R} into the objective in Eq. B.1 and applying the identities in Eqs. B.3 to B.7, up to a constant independent of 𝑳\bm{L} and 𝑹\bm{R},

Φt​(𝑳,𝑹)=\displaystyle\Phi_{t}(\bm{L},\bm{R})=\; tr⁡(𝑳​𝒀t⊤​𝑹​𝒀t)+tr⁡(𝑳−1​𝑺t⊤​𝑹−1​𝑺t)\displaystyle\operatorname{tr}(\bm{L}\bm{Y}_{t}^{\top}\bm{R}\bm{Y}_{t})+\operatorname{tr}(\bm{L}^{-1}\bm{S}_{t}^{\top}\bm{R}^{-1}\bm{S}_{t})
+1λ​tr⁡(𝑳t​𝑳−1)​tr⁡(𝑹t​𝑹−1)+1λ​[n​log​det𝑳+m​log​det𝑹].\displaystyle+\tfrac{1}{\lambda}\operatorname{tr}(\bm{L}_{t}\bm{L}^{-1})\operatorname{tr}(\bm{R}_{t}\bm{R}^{-1})+\tfrac{1}{\lambda}\left[n\log\det\bm{L}+m\log\det\bm{R}\right]. (B.13)

This expression makes the dependence on each factor explicit. We minimize it first over 𝑳\bm{L} with 𝑹=𝑹t\bm{R}=\bm{R}_{t}, then over 𝑹\bm{R} with 𝑳=𝑳t+1\bm{L}=\bm{L}_{t+1} fixed.

Holding 𝑹=𝑹t\bm{R}=\bm{R}_{t} fixed and collecting terms in Eq. B.13 involving 𝑳\bm{L}, we obtain the conditional update

𝑳t+1=arg​min𝐋∈𝕊+⁣+mtr(𝐔L𝐋)+tr(𝐕L𝐋−1)+logdet𝐋.\displaystyle\bm{L}_{t+1}=\argmin_{\bm{L}\in\mathbb{S}_{\scalebox{0.7}{$\scriptscriptstyle++$}}^{m}}\quad\operatorname{tr}(\bm{U}_{L}\bm{L})+\operatorname{tr}(\bm{V}_{L}\bm{L}^{-1})+\log\det\bm{L}. (B.14)

Differentiating the objective in Eq. B.14 with respect to 𝑳\bm{L} and setting the derivative to zero yields the quadratic matrix equation

𝑳​𝑼L​𝑳+𝑳=𝑽L.\displaystyle\bm{L}\,\bm{U}_{L}\,\bm{L}+\bm{L}=\bm{V}_{L}. (B.15)

Here, because 𝑼L⪰0\bm{U}_{L}\succeq 0 and 𝑽L≻0\bm{V}_{L}\succ 0, this equation has a positive-definite solution 𝑳t+1\bm{L}_{t+1} (Lemma B.4). To establish uniqueness, we appeal to the observation that the objective is strictly convex in 𝑳−1\bm{L}^{-1}.

We then update the factor 𝑹\bm{R} in an analogous manner, holding 𝑳t+1\bm{L}_{t+1} fixed:

𝑹t+1=arg​min𝐑∈𝕊+⁣+ntr(𝐔R𝐑)+tr(𝐕R𝐑−1)+logdet𝐑,\displaystyle\bm{R}_{t+1}=\argmin_{\bm{R}\in\mathbb{S}_{\scalebox{0.7}{$\scriptscriptstyle++$}}^{n}}\quad\operatorname{tr}(\bm{U}_{R}\bm{R})+\operatorname{tr}(\bm{V}_{R}\bm{R}^{-1})+\log\det\bm{R}, (B.16)

Solving Eq. B.16 for 𝑹t+1\bm{R}_{t+1} reduces to solving another quadratic matrix equation

𝑹​𝑼R​𝑹+𝑹=𝑽R,\displaystyle\bm{R}\,\bm{U}_{R}\,\bm{R}+\bm{R}=\bm{V}_{R}, (B.17)

which again has a unique, positive-definite solution.

Each block update minimizes the objective over one factor, holding the other factor and the reference matrix 𝑯t\bm{H}_{t} fixed. Since the current factor is feasible, each update cannot increase the objective. Forming the coefficient products costs 𝒪⁡(n2​m+n​m2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}m+nm^{2}); the factor inverses and two quadratric matrix equation solves cost 𝒪⁡(n3+m3)\mathcal{O}(n^{3}+m^{3}). ∎

B.3 Quadratic Matrix Equations

In the previous Section B.2 we showed that SoftServe-Kron has an alternating update for the factors 𝑳\bm{L} and 𝑹\bm{R}, where first we perform

\tcboxmath[equationbox,title=]Update 𝑳t+1 by solving 𝑳𝑼L𝑳+𝑳=𝑽L,\displaystyle\tcboxmath[equationbox,title={}]{\text{Update~$\bm{L}_{t+1}$~by~solving~}\bm{L}\,\bm{U}_{L}\,\bm{L}+\bm{L}=\bm{V}_{L},} (B.18)

and then we perform the update

\tcboxmath[equationbox,title=]Update 𝑹t+1 by solving 𝑹𝑼R𝑹+𝑹=𝑽R.\displaystyle\tcboxmath[equationbox,title={}]{\text{Update~$\bm{R}_{t+1}$~by~solving~}\bm{R}\,\bm{U}_{R}\,\bm{R}+\bm{R}=\bm{V}_{R}.} (B.19)

Given known matrices 𝑼⪰0\bm{U}\succeq 0 and 𝑽≻0\bm{V}\succ 0, each update above involves solving a quadratic matrix equation of the form

\tcboxmath[equationbox,title=]𝑸𝑼𝑸+𝑸=𝑽.\displaystyle\tcboxmath[equationbox,title={}]{\bm{Q}\bm{U}\bm{Q}+\bm{Q}=\bm{V}.} (B.20)

Cai et al. (2024, Lemma B.2) show that Eq. B.21 below is the positive definite solution.

B.4Quadratic matrix equation.

The positive definite solution to Eq. B.20 is given by

𝑸=2​𝑽1/2​[𝑰+(𝑰+4​𝑽1/2​𝑼​𝑽1/2)1/2]−1​𝑽1/2.\bm{Q}=2\bm{V}^{1/2}\left[\bm{I}+\left(\bm{I}+4\bm{V}^{1/2}\bm{U}\bm{V}^{1/2}\right)^{1/2}\right]^{-1}\bm{V}^{1/2}. (B.21)

When updating either Kronecker factor, 𝑳\bm{L} or 𝑹\bm{R}, the matrix 𝑼\bm{U} in Eq. B.20 admits a Gram factorization 𝑼=𝑭​𝑭⊤\bm{U}=\bm{F}\bm{F}^{\top}. Cai et al. (2024, Lemma B.3) (see also Modi et al. (2025)) provide an equivalent expression for the solution to the quadratic matrix equation in Eq. B.20 in terms of this Gram matrix, which is given by

\tcboxmath[equationbox,title=]𝑸=𝑽−𝑽⊤𝑭[12𝑰+(𝑭⊤𝑽𝑭+14𝑰)12]−2𝑭⊤𝑽.\displaystyle\tcboxmath[equationbox,title={}]{\bm{Q}=\bm{V}-\bm{V}^{\top}\bm{F}\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\bm{I}+(\bm{F}^{\top}\bm{V}\bm{F}+\tfrac{1}{4}\bm{I})^{\frac{1}{2}}\right]^{-2}\bm{F}^{\top}\bm{V}.} (B.22)

For a matrix 𝑭∈ℝd×p\bm{F}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times p}, this update takes 𝒪⁡(d2​p+p3)\mathcal{O}(d^{2}p+p^{3}) computation.

Our implementation of SoftServe-Kron, which relies on the coupled Newton-Schulz, will rely on the latter Gram form of the solution in Eq. B.22.

Appendix C SoftServe: numerical computation of Kronecker updates

The Kronecker updates in Section 3.2 require solving two quadratic matrix equations, one for each factor. In this section, we describe how to evaluate these updates using matrix multiplications and Newton-Schulz iterations, as outlined in Section 4.1. We begin by explaining how to form the coefficients 𝑼,𝑽\bm{U},\bm{V} of the quadratic matrix equations, then we describe the Newton-Schulz procedures, and finally we explain how to apply the Newton-Schulz procedures to obtain the full Gram update, providing explicit pseudocode for the Kronecker factor updates 𝑳\bm{L} and 𝑹\bm{R}.

C.1 Evaluating the updates in Gram form

In this section, we show that the coefficients 𝑼=𝑭​𝑭⊤\bm{U}=\bm{F}\bm{F}^{\top} and 𝑽\bm{V} can be written in terms of matrix multiplications and square root and inverse square root operations. Consider the Gram solution to the quadratic matrix equation in Eq. B.22. This expression requires a square root of 𝑪=𝑭⊤​𝑽​𝑭+14​𝑰\bm{C}=\bm{F}^{\top}\bm{V}\bm{F}+\tfrac{1}{4}\bm{I} and an inverse of 12​𝑰+𝑪12\tfrac{1}{2}\bm{I}+\bm{C}^{\frac{1}{2}}. Overall, this solution requires fewer matrix function evaluations (i.e., square root and inverse) than the solution in Eq. B.21.

We begin by motivating the Gram update further by examining the factorization 𝑼=𝑭​𝑭⊤\bm{U}=\bm{F}\bm{F}^{\top}. For our Kronecker factor updates, we recall the definitions of 𝑼L\bm{U}_{L} and 𝑼R\bm{U}_{R} in Eqs. B.11 and B.12,

𝑼L\displaystyle\bm{U}_{L} =λn​𝒀t⊤​𝑹t​𝒀t\displaystyle=\tfrac{\lambda}{n}\bm{Y}_{t}^{\top}\bm{R}_{t}\bm{Y}_{t}\quad (C.1)
𝑼R\displaystyle\bm{U}_{R} =λm​𝒀t​𝑳t+1​𝒀t⊤.\displaystyle=\tfrac{\lambda}{m}\bm{Y}_{t}\bm{L}_{t+1}\bm{Y}_{t}^{\top}. (C.2)

Thus, the required factorizations arise from

𝑼L\displaystyle\bm{U}_{L} =𝑭L​𝑭L⊤,𝑭L=λn​𝒀t⊤​𝑹t12\displaystyle=\bm{F}_{L}\bm{F}_{L}^{\top},\qquad\bm{F}_{L}=\sqrt{\tfrac{\lambda}{n}}\bm{Y}_{t}^{\top}\bm{R}_{t}^{\frac{1}{2}} (C.3)
𝑼R\displaystyle\bm{U}_{R} =𝑭R​𝑭R⊤,𝑭R=λm​𝒀t​𝑳t+112.\displaystyle=\bm{F}_{R}\bm{F}_{R}^{\top},\qquad\bm{F}_{R}=\sqrt{\tfrac{\lambda}{m}}\bm{Y}_{t}\bm{L}_{t+1}^{\frac{1}{2}}. (C.4)

The remaining coefficients 𝑽L\bm{V}_{L} and 𝑽R\bm{V}_{R} can be formed with the corresponding inverse square roots to the square roots used above. For example, for 𝑽L=𝑳t+λn​𝑺t⊤​𝑹t−1​𝑺t\bm{V}_{L}=\bm{L}_{t}+\tfrac{\lambda}{n}\bm{S}_{t}^{\top}\bm{R}_{t}^{-1}\bm{S}_{t}, we can form the second term using

𝑺t⊤​𝑹t−1​𝑺t=(𝑹t−12​𝑺t)⊤​(𝑹t−12​𝑺t).\displaystyle\bm{S}_{t}^{\top}\bm{R}_{t}^{-1}\bm{S}_{t}=(\bm{R}_{t}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\bm{S}_{t})^{\top}(\bm{R}_{t}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\bm{S}_{t}). (C.5)

This construction allows us to reuse both outputs of each coupled Newton-Schulz call: the square root forms 𝑭L\bm{F}_{L} (or OPEN𝑭R)\bm{F}_{R}), and the corresponding inverse square root forms 𝑽L\bm{V}_{L} (or 𝑽R\bm{V}_{R}), avoiding a separate Newton-Schulz call to approximate the inverse 𝑹t−1\bm{R}_{t}^{-1}.

In Algorithm C.2, we summarize how to form all of the coefficients in this manner.

C.2 Newton-Schulz for the square root and inverse

To compute the Gram solution of the quadratic matrix equation, we need an approximation for the matrix square root and the matrix inverse. We approximate the required matrix functions using Newton-Schulz iterations, which construct polynomial approximations through repeated matrix multiplications and additions. We summarize these routines in Algorithm C.1 as NewtonSchulzRootPair and NewtonSchulzInverse, respectively.

For square roots, we use the coupled Newton-Schulz iteration, which simultaneously approximates a matrix square root and its inverse using matrix multiplications (Higham, 1997; Higham, 2008). For an input matrix 𝑴∈𝕊+⁣+d\bm{M}\in\mathbb{S}_{\scalebox{0.7}{$\scriptscriptstyle++$}}^{d}, let ‖𝑴‖F\|\bm{M}\|_{F} denote its Frobenius norm. First, we rescale the matrix ‖𝑴‖F\|\bm{M}\|_{F}, placing the eigenvalues between 00 and 11:

a\displaystyle a =‖𝑴‖F,\displaystyle=\|\bm{M}\|_{F}, (C.6)
𝒁0\displaystyle\bm{Z}_{0} =𝑴/a,\displaystyle=\bm{M}/a, (C.7)
𝑷0\displaystyle\bm{P}_{0} =𝑰.\displaystyle=\bm{I}. (C.8)

In the Newton-Schulz procedure, we then iterate j=0,…,J−1j=0,\ldots,J-1 times through

𝑻j\displaystyle\bm{T}_{j} =12​(3​𝑰−𝑷j​𝒁j)\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}(3\bm{I}-\bm{P}_{j}\bm{Z}_{j}) (C.9)
𝒁j+1\displaystyle\bm{Z}_{j+1} =sym​[𝒁j​𝑻j]\displaystyle=\text{sym}[\bm{Z}_{j}\bm{T}_{j}] (C.10)
𝑷j+1\displaystyle\bm{P}_{j+1} =sym​[𝑻j​𝑷j],\displaystyle=\text{sym}[\bm{T}_{j}\bm{P}_{j}], (C.11)

where we define the matrix symmetrization operation

sym​[𝑨]=(𝑨+𝑨⊤)/2.\displaystyle\text{sym}[\bm{A}]=(\bm{A}+\bm{A}^{\top})/2. (C.12)

The iterates 𝒁j\bm{Z}_{j} and 𝑷j\bm{P}_{j} approximate the square root and inverse square root, respectively, of the scaled input. The correction 𝑻j=12​(3​𝑰−𝑷j​𝒁j)\bm{T}_{j}=\tfrac{1}{2}(3\bm{I}-\bm{P}_{j}\bm{Z}_{j}) is a first-degree polynomial in 𝑷j​𝒁j\bm{P}_{j}\bm{Z}_{j}.

After JJ iterations, rescaling by a\sqrt{a} gives the desired approximations with respect to the original input matrix are given by

𝑴12\displaystyle\bm{M}^{\frac{1}{2}} ≈a​𝒁J\displaystyle\approx\sqrt{a}\,\bm{Z}_{J} (C.13)
𝑴−12\displaystyle\bm{M}^{-\frac{1}{2}} ≈𝑷J/a.\displaystyle\approx\bm{P}_{J}/\sqrt{a}. (C.14)

To approximate the inverse of the matrix, we apply a separate Newton-Schulz iteration (Schulz, 1933; Higham, 2008). For a positive definite matrix 𝑴∈𝕊+⁣+d\bm{M}\in\mathbb{S}_{\scalebox{0.7}{$\scriptscriptstyle++$}}^{d}, we initialize and then iterate j=0,…,J−1j=0,\ldots,J-1 times

𝑬0\displaystyle\bm{E}_{0} =𝑰/‖𝑴‖F\displaystyle=\bm{I}/\|\bm{M}\|_{F} (C.15)
𝑬j+1\displaystyle\bm{E}_{j+1} =sym⁡[𝑬j​(2​𝑰−𝑴​𝑬j)].\displaystyle=\operatorname{sym}[\bm{E}_{j}(2\bm{I}-\bm{M}\bm{E}_{j})]. (C.16)

This update builds a polynomial approximation to 𝑴−1\bm{M}^{-1}. After JJ iterations, we return the approximation 𝑬J≈𝑴−1\bm{E}_{J}\approx\bm{M}^{-1}.

C.3 Computing the Kronecker updates via Newton-Schulz

We now combine the Newton-Schulz routines to evaluate the Gram update in Eq. B.22. Given 𝑭\bm{F} and 𝑽\bm{V}, we form 𝑪=𝑭⊤​𝑽​𝑭+14​𝑰\bm{C}=\bm{F}^{\top}\bm{V}\bm{F}+\tfrac{1}{4}\bm{I} and apply NewtonSchulzRootPair to obtain an approximation 𝑩^≈𝑪12\widehat{\bm{B}}\approx\bm{C}^{\frac{1}{2}}. We then apply NewtonSchulzInverse to obtain 𝑾^≈(12​𝑰+𝑩^)−1\widehat{\bm{W}}\approx(\tfrac{1}{2}\bm{I}+\widehat{\bm{B}})^{-1}. The resulting Newton-Schulz approximation to the Gram solution (B.22) of the quadratic matrix equation is then given by

𝑸^=𝑽−(𝑽​𝑭​𝑾^)​(𝑽​𝑭​𝑾^)⊤.\displaystyle\widehat{\bm{Q}}=\bm{V}-(\bm{V}\bm{F}{\widehat{\bm{W}}})(\bm{V}\bm{F}{\widehat{\bm{W}}})^{\top}. (C.17)

The resulting update only requires these two Newton-Schulz routines and matrix multiplications. Algorithm C.2 presents the pseudocode for this Gram update and its application within the alternating Kronecker update for the factors 𝑳\bm{L} and 𝑹\bm{R}. In our implementation, we use 18 iterations for the square root routines, and 10 for the inverse routine.

In the application of these procedures to the quadratic matrix equation solution, our implementation symmetrizes every output and, for every solve, records the normalized residual

ρQ=‖𝑸​𝑼​𝑸+𝑸−𝑽‖F/‖𝑽‖F,\rho_{Q}=\left\lVert\bm{Q}\bm{U}\bm{Q}+\bm{Q}-\bm{V}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}/\left\lVert\bm{V}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}},

so we can verify how close we are to the exact solution to the quadratic matrix equation.

Appendix D Optimizer Details

D.1 Training with SoftServe

We provide more of the details of how our SoftServe methods are implemented. In particular, this section will explain the detailed pseudo code of SoftServe-Kron and SoftServe-Diag is in Algorithm D.1 and Algorithm D.2, respectively.

SoftServe-Kron is a method for updating matrix parameters, where we will use 𝑿∈ℝn×m{\bm{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} to denote the matrix parameters of a given layer. Whereas SoftServe-Diag is applicable to parameters of any shape, and thus in Algorithm D.2, we represent the given parameters as a vector x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. If this corresponds to a linear layer, then d=n​md=nm, where n×mn\times m are the dimensions of the linear layer.

To make SoftServe practical, we will make use of some now-standard practices in deep learning, including the use of momentum, updating the approximate Hessian every so often to amortize costs, and taking care to properly scale the update directions. We address each of these considerations in turn.

To estimate the gradient for the quasi-Newton step, we will use momentum estimate which in matrix form is updated according to lines (7–8) in Algorithm D.1, and in vector form is updated according to lines (7–8) in Algorithm D.2. We also incorporate an additional Nesterov extrapolation or the debiasing trick Kingma and Ba (2015) to form the final momentum estimate.

Restricting the Hessian approximation to a diagonal or Kronecker factor greatly reduces the costs as compared to the dense Soft QN method. For instance, for a n×mn\times m linear layer, the state, application, and refresh costs of SoftServe are given in Table D.1.

In particular, the cost for applying and refreshing the Kronecker-factored update in SoftServe-Kron is still cubic in the dimensions of the layer. To amortize this cost, we will update our estimate of the inverse Hessian only once every K∈ℕK\in\mathbb{N} iterations. That is, once every KK iterations we take a snapshot of the current iterate, gradient, and sample in line 6 in Algorithm D.1. We then use this snap shot to form our difference of iterates 𝑺\bm{S} and gradients 𝒀\bm{Y} on lines 11 and 12. The analogous snapshot for and its application for SoftServe-Diag are on lines 6, 11 and 12 in Algorithm D.2.

The differences of iterates and gradients are then used to update the factorized and diagonal Hessian estimates on line 13 of Algorithm D.1 and line 13 of Algorithm D.2, respectively. To be more efficient (or pythonic) we have written the update of the diagonal estimate ht+1h_{t+1} on line 13 in Algorithm D.2 as a vector operation as opposed to an element-wise operation as introduced in Eq. 6.

Our final modification to make SoftServe practical for deep learning is to normalize the update. We will explain this modification for a vector parameter x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. The same modification for matrix parameters follows by vectorizing, and then re-stacking as a matrix. Traditionally quasi-Newton methods are applied according to

xt+1=xt−γt​𝑯t​m^t.x_{t+1}=x_{t}-\gamma_{t}\bm{H}_{t}\hat{m}_{t}. (D.2)

This update Eq. D.2 corresponds to the regularized descent method:

xt+1=arg⁡minx∈ℝd​m^t⊤​(x−xt)+12​γt​‖x−xt‖𝑯t−12.\displaystyle x_{t+1}=\underset{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}{\arg\min}\;\;\hat{m}_{t}^{\top}(x-x_{t})+\tfrac{1}{2\gamma_{t}}\|x-x_{t}\|_{\bm{H}_{t}^{-1}}^{2}.

But now there is a growing body of evidence that the constrained descent method (Jordan et al., 2024; Pethick et al., 2025; Crawshaw et al., 2026) given by

xt+1\displaystyle x_{t+1} =arg⁡minx∈ℝd​m^t⊤​(x−xt)subject to ​‖x−xt‖𝑯t−1≤γt\displaystyle=\underset{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}{\arg\min}\;\;\hat{m}_{t}^{\top}(x-x_{t})\quad\mbox{subject to }\|x-x_{t}\|_{\bm{H}_{t}^{-1}}\leq\gamma_{t}
=xt−γt​𝑯t​m^t/m^t⊤​𝑯t​m^t\displaystyle=x_{t}-\gamma_{t}\bm{H}_{t}\hat{m}_{t}\big/\sqrt{\hat{m}_{t}^{\top}\bm{H}_{t}\hat{m}_{t}} (D.3)

generally works better for deep learning. Our initial experiments also confirmed that the constrained descent Eq. D.3 resulting in better methods and thus we used Eq. D.3 throughout our experiments to update the parameters; see line 9 of Algorithm D.1 and line 9 of Algorithm D.2.

In these updates, note that the product 𝑯t​m^t\bm{H}_{t}\hat{m}_{t} in Eq. D.3 is given by

𝑯t​m^t={vec⁡(𝑹t​𝑴^t​𝑳t)in line 9 in Algorithm D.1 ,ht⊙m^tin line 9 in Algorithm D.2 ,\bm{H}_{t}\hat{m}_{t}=\begin{cases}\operatorname{vec}\!\big(\bm{R}_{t}\hat{\bm{M}}_{t}\bm{L}_{t}\big)&\mbox{in line~\ref{ln:update-kron} in~\lx@cref{creftypecap~refnum}{alg:softserve-kron} },\\ h_{t}\odot\hat{m}_{t}&\mbox{in line~\ref{ln:update-d} in~\lx@cref{creftypecap~refnum}{alg:softserve-diag} },\end{cases} (D.4)

where the Kronecker case follows from Eq. B.4, and ⊙\odot is the elementwise (Hadamard) product.

D.2 Routing and state

The parameter partition is disjoint. A Diag block stores one positive value per coordinate; a Kron block for an n×mn\times m matrix stores 𝑳∈𝕊+⁣+m\bm{L}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{m} and 𝑹∈𝕊+⁣+n\bm{R}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{n}. Blocks without a matrix interpretation are routed to Diag, or to a first-order fallback in the neural experiments (Appendix E). Kron factors of equal shape are stacked for batched matrix multiplication. The initial states are h0=𝟏h_{0}=\mathbf{1}, the all-ones vector, and (𝑳0,𝑹0)=(𝑰m,𝑰n)(\bm{L}_{0},\bm{R}_{0})=(\bm{I}_{m},\bm{I}_{n}). The metric is fixed within each interval of KK parameter steps. Each refresh uses one raw interval pair; we do not average pairs or interpolate metric states.

D.3 Replay and gradient accounting

A replay key stores every random choice that affects fζtf_{\zeta_{t}}: the minibatch indices, augmentation, dropout masks, and any other sampled loss input. Replaying the key at both endpoints removes sampling mismatch from yty_{t}. The replayed gradient is used only for the refresh; it does not update momentum, the learning-rate schedule, or the parameters. For NN parameter steps, Algorithm D.1 evaluates NN ordinary gradients and ⌊(N−1)/K⌋\lfloor(N-1)/K\rfloor replayed ones, and we count both. With decoupled weight decay, the displacement sts_{t} is the actual parameter displacement, including the decay. A checkpoint taken inside an interval must retain the momentum, the metric state, the interval start, the cached raw gradient, and the replay key.

Appendix E Experimental Details and Additional Results

E.1 Experimental setting

Hardware and arithmetic.

We use NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs for training. Models use FP32, with BF16 autocasting for GPT.

Selection and evaluation.

We tune learning rates on seed 0 using logarithmic grids, extending a grid when its minimum lies at the boundary. Final runs use seeds 1–3. Within each task, methods share initialization seeds and data. Test errors are not used for selection. Curves show three-seed means and variability bands; settings with failed seeds are shown as individual traces.

RNN Adding, MNIST, and the small PINNs screen the first-moment coefficient β1\beta_{1} for SoftServe, SoftServe-I, Adam, Muon, and SOAP. K-FAC and K-BFGS(L) also receive a momentum search. In these studies, Nesterov on/off is tested for SoftServe and Muon; Adam and SOAP retain the momentum update rules of their implementations while their β1\beta_{1} values are tuned. The task descriptions below specify which settings are tuned or fixed.

Optimizer settings.

SoftServe uses K=10K=10, and one alternating factor sweep per refresh. Kron uses the Gram QME implementation in Algorithm C.2, with 18 coupled root iterations and 10 inverse iterations; Diag uses the closed-form elementwise update.

Gradient accounting and plots.

Gradient budgets count training gradients, secant replays, line-search evaluations, and loss-balancing gradients. In stochastic training, replay adds approximately 10% to SoftServe-Kron’s count at K=10K=10, so it takes fewer parameter updates within the same budget.

E.2 RNN Adding

Task and data.

Each length-TT input has T=100T=100 pairs zτ=(aτ,mτ)z_{\tau}=(a_{\tau},m_{\tau}), where aτ∼Uniform⁡[0,1]a_{\tau}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}[0,1]. Exactly two markers mτm_{\tau} equal one, one in each half of the sequence. The target is the sum of the marked numbers. Every update draws 128 new sequences; validation and test sets each contain 8,192 fixed sequences per seed.

Model and objective.

The network uses hτ=tanh⁡(Wh​hτ−1+Wz​zτ+b)h_{\tau}=\tanh(W_{h}h_{\tau-1}+W_{z}z_{\tau}+b), hidden width 16, h0=0h_{0}=0, and a scalar affine readout, for 321 parameters. The target and batch loss are

y=∑τ=1Tmτ​aτ,ℒ⁡(θ)=1B​∑i=1B(y^θ​(z(i))−y(i))2.y=\sum_{\tau=1}^{T}m_{\tau}a_{\tau},\qquad\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\bigl(\widehat{y}_{\theta}(z^{(i)})-y^{(i)}\bigr)^{2}. (E.1)

Here BB is the batch size and y^θ\widehat{y}_{\theta} is the prediction.

Training and tuning.

The budget is 40,000 gradient evaluations. An 8,000-gradient pilot screens hyperparameters, followed by full-budget learning-rate sweeps selected by validation MSE (Figure E.1). The selected values are λ=999\lambda=999 for SoftServe-Kron and λ=1\lambda=1 for SoftServe-Diag.

Evaluation.

We report minibatch training MSE and fixed-set validation and test MSE. Figure E.2 shows training and validation MSE against parameter updates and wall-clock time. K-BFGS(L)’s two failed seeds are shown individually.

Local conditioning.

We compute the full 321×321321\times 321 loss Hessian at initialization on a fixed batch of 128 sequences for each of seeds 0–3, using FP64 differentiation. All four Hessians are indefinite. Each has one to six singular values below 321​ε64​σmax321\varepsilon_{64}\sigma_{\max}, where ε64=2−52\varepsilon_{64}=2^{-52} and σmax\sigma_{\max} is the largest singular value. Thus, these sampled losses are numerically nearly singular at initialization; a finite condition number cannot be resolved reliably (Figure E.3).

E.3 MNIST autoencoder

Task and data.

We use MNIST, comprising 28×2828\times 28 grayscale images of handwritten digits, with 60,000 training and 10,000 test examples and pixel values in [0,1][0,1]. The task is to compress each image into a low-dimensional representation and reconstruct the original input, without using digit labels. This autoencoder task is a standard benchmark for second-order optimization (Goldfarb et al., 2020).

Model and objective.

We use a 2.8M-parameter fully connected autoencoder with a symmetric encoder–decoder architecture and a 30-dimensional linear bottleneck. The remaining hidden layers use ReLU, and the output uses sigmoid. Following Goldfarb et al. (2020), the batch objective is

ℒ(θ)=−1B∑i=1B∑j=1784[xi​jlogx^i​j+(1−xi​j)log(1−x^i​j)]+10−52∥θ∥22,\mathcal{L}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\sum_{j=1}^{784}\left[x_{ij}\log\widehat{x}_{ij}+(1-x_{ij})\log(1-\widehat{x}_{ij})\right]+\frac{10^{-5}}{2}\|\theta\|_{2}^{2}, (E.2)

where BB is the batch size, xx is the input image, and x^\widehat{x} is its reconstruction.

Training and tuning.

Full-batch training uses 4,000 gradient evaluations; minibatch training uses batches of 1,000 images and 6,000 evaluations. SoftServe-Kron, SoftServe-I, Muon, and SOAP use Adam on biases, while SoftServe-Diag acts on all parameters. Full-batch L-BFGS uses a strong-Wolfe line search.

A quarter-budget pilot screens hyperparameters, followed by full-budget learning-rate sweeps selected by the mean of the final five training objectives (Figure E.4). We select λ=999\lambda=999 for SoftServe-Kron and λ=9\lambda=9 for SoftServe-Diag.

Evaluation.

Figure E.5 reports test reconstruction BCE, excluding the training regularizer. Figure E.6 shows the regularized training objective against parameter updates and wall-clock time. Failed runs are shown individually rather than included in three-seed means.

E.4 Small physics-informed neural networks

Task and data.

We consider three one-dimensional problems from Rathore et al. (2024). The scalar function u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) denotes the solution at spatial coordinate xx and time tt. All problems use t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1].

Convection. On the spatial domain [0,2​π][0,2\pi], we solve

∂u∂t+40​∂u∂x\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}+40\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} =0,\displaystyle=0,
u⁡(x,0)\displaystyle u(x,0) =sin⁡x,\displaystyle=\sin x,
u⁡(0,t)\displaystyle u(0,t) =u⁡(2​π,t).\displaystyle=u(2\pi,t).

The analytical solution is

u⋆​(x,t)=sin⁡(x−40​t).u^{\star}(x,t)=\sin(x-40t).

Reaction. On the spatial domain [0,2​π][0,2\pi], we solve

∂u∂t−5​u​(1−u)\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}-5u(1-u) =0,\displaystyle=0,
u⁡(x,0)\displaystyle u(x,0) =h⁡(x),\displaystyle=h(x),
u⁡(0,t)\displaystyle u(0,t) =u⁡(2​π,t),\displaystyle=u(2\pi,t),

where h(x)=exp[−(x−π)2/(2(π/4)2)]h(x)=\exp[-(x-\pi)^{2}/(2(\pi/4)^{2})]. The analytical solution is

u⋆​(x,t)=h⁡(x)​e5​th⁡(x)​e5​t+1−h⁡(x).u^{\star}(x,t)=\frac{h(x)e^{5t}}{h(x)e^{5t}+1-h(x)}.

Wave. On the spatial domain [0,1][0,1], we solve

∂2u∂t2−4​∂2u∂x2\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial t^{2}}-4\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial x^{2}} =0,\displaystyle=0,
u⁡(x,0)\displaystyle u(x,0) =sin⁡(π​x)+12​sin⁡(5​π​x),\displaystyle=\sin(\pi x)+\tfrac{1}{2}\sin(5\pi x),
∂u∂t​(x,0)\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}(x,0) =0,\displaystyle=0,
u⁡(0,t)=u⁡(1,t)\displaystyle u(0,t)=u(1,t) =0.\displaystyle=0.

The analytical solution is

u⋆​(x,t)=sin⁡(π​x)​cos⁡(2​π​t)+12​sin⁡(5​π​x)​cos⁡(10​π​t).u^{\star}(x,t)=\sin(\pi x)\cos(2\pi t)+\tfrac{1}{2}\sin(5\pi x)\cos(10\pi t).

The analytical solutions are used to evaluate solution errors, not as interior training targets.

Model and objective.

We use a fully connected network with three width-200 tanh hidden layers and 81,201 parameters to predict uθ​(x,t)u_{\theta}(x,t). The training objective is

ℒ⁡(θ)=ℒPDE+ℒIC+ℒBC.\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PDE}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IC}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BC}}.

The PDE term is the mean squared equation residual. The initial- and boundary-condition terms sum the MSEs for the prescribed conditions. For Wave, these include both initial displacement and velocity, and the values at both spatial boundaries.

Training and tuning.

We use 200,000 gradient evaluations and cosine learning-rate decay to one tenth of the initial rate. In the deterministic setting, the 10,000 interior collocation points remain fixed throughout training. In the stochastic setting, they are resampled at every update. Both gradients of each secant pair are evaluated on the same points.

Following hyperparameter screening, we select learning rates by the mean of the final five training losses (Figure E.7). SoftServe-Kron uses β1=0.995\beta_{1}=0.995. For Wave, Convection, and Reaction, respectively, its selected λ\lambda values are (99,9999,999)(99,9999,999) in the deterministic setting and 99 for all three in the stochastic setting. In the same problem order, SoftServe-Diag uses (9,1,1)(9,1,1) for deterministic training and (9,1,9)(9,1,9) for stochastic training.

SoftServe-Kron, SoftServe-I, Muon, and SOAP update the two 200×200200\times 200 hidden weight matrices, with Adam on the remaining parameters. Deterministic experiments also include L-BFGS and Adam followed by L-BFGS, using strong-Wolfe line searches.

Evaluation.

We measure relative solution error,

‖uθ−u⋆‖2‖u⋆‖2,\frac{\|u_{\theta}-u^{\star}\|_{2}}{\|u^{\star}\|_{2}},

with both solutions evaluated on a 129×101129\times 101 space–time grid. Figure E.8 reports FP32 solution errors. Figures E.11 and E.12 show training losses against parameter updates and wall-clock time.

Since numerical precision can affect PINN convergence (Xu et al., 2025), we repeat the experiments in FP64 using the FP32-selected configurations without retuning. Figures E.9 and E.10 report the corresponding training losses and solution errors. Failed runs are shown individually. When an L-BFGS line search returns zero displacement, we extend its final value horizontally to indicate that the iterate remains unchanged.

E.5 PirateNet

Task and data.

We solve the Allen–Cahn and Korteweg–de Vries (KdV) equations on (x,t)∈[−1,1]×[0,1](x,t)\in[-1,1]\times[0,1], where u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) is the scalar solution.

Allen–Cahn.

∂u∂t−10−4​∂2u∂x2+5​u3−5​u\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}-10^{-4}\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial x^{2}}+5u^{3}-5u =0,\displaystyle=0,
u⁡(x,0)\displaystyle u(x,0) =x2​cos⁡(π​x).\displaystyle=x^{2}\cos(\pi x).

KdV.

∂u∂t+u​∂u∂x+0.0222​∂3u∂x3\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}+u\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+0.022^{2}\frac{\partial^{3}u}{\partial x^{3}} =0,\displaystyle=0,
u⁡(x,0)\displaystyle u(x,0) =cos⁡(π​x).\displaystyle=\cos(\pi x).

Both problems use periodic spatial boundaries. Reference solutions for evaluation are taken from the jaxpi repository.11 1 https://github.com/PredictiveIntelligenceLab/jaxpi

Model and objective.

We use PirateNet (Wang et al., 2024), a residual PINN with three width-256 blocks, tanh activations, and approximately 0.73M parameters. The network uses periodic spatial features, and its final layer is initialized by least squares against the initial condition.

Following Wang et al. (2025), training minimizes a weighted combination of PDE residual and initial-condition MSEs. Causal weighting prioritizes earlier times, while gradient-norm balancing adjusts the relative weights of the loss terms. These weights are treated as constants during differentiation and held fixed between the two secant evaluations.

Training and tuning.

Each update samples 32,768 uniform collocation points. We compare methods at 300,600 gradient evaluations for Allen–Cahn and 100,200 for KdV, counting both secant replay and loss-balancing gradients. Learning rates use a 5,000-update warmup followed by exponential decay. Matrix methods use β1=0.995\beta_{1}=0.995 and Adam on the remaining parameters. Momentum settings are fixed during tuning.

Learning-rate sweeps run for 300,000 updates on Allen–Cahn and 100,000 on KdV, with selection based on unweighted validation loss (Figure E.13). The selected λ\lambda values for SoftServe-Kron are λ=9999\lambda=9999 for Allen–Cahn and λ=999\lambda=999 for KdV.

Evaluation.

Although all optimizers use the same weighting rules, their training weights evolve differently. We therefore compare the unweighted sum of PDE and initial-condition MSEs on common fixed points. Figure E.14 shows this loss against parameter updates and wall-clock time.

Figure E.15 reports relative L2L^{2} solution errors on the reference grid. Solution errors are not used for learning-rate selection. All curves stop at the same gradient budgets as the main figures, so SoftServe-Kron takes fewer parameter updates because of replay.

E.6 Physics-informed diffusion

Task and data.

We consider structural design using the mechanics dataset of Bastek et al. (2025), which contains 30,000 optimized structures. Given supports, applied loads, and a material budget, the model generates a material-density field and two displacement fields. We retain the released 65×6565\times 65 field representation and 64×6464\times 64 finite-element grid.

Model and objective.

We use the released 136M-parameter U-Net, consisting of residual convolution blocks and attention layers. It predicts the two displacement fields and the material density, with a sigmoid output for density.

Let z0z_{0} contain the target fields and cc the design conditions. At diffusion timestep tt, we construct a noisy input

zt=α¯t​z0+1−α¯t​ε,ε∼𝒩⁡(0,I),z_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}z_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\varepsilon,\qquad\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I),

where α¯t\bar{\alpha}_{t} is the cumulative signal-retention factor. The network predicts the clean fields as z^0=fθ​(zt,t,c)\widehat{z}_{0}=f_{\theta}(z_{t},t,c). The training objective combines reconstruction and physics-based terms:

ℒ⁡(θ)=𝔼⁡[wt​MSE⁡(z^0,z0)+ℓt​(req)+10​ℓt​(rvol)+10−4​C].\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[w_{t}\,\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat{z}_{0},z_{0})+\ell_{t}(r_{\mathrm{eq}})+10\,\ell_{t}(r_{\mathrm{vol}})+10^{-4}C\right]. (E.3)

The expectation is over training examples, diffusion timesteps, and noise. The equilibrium residual is

req=K⁡(ρ^)​u^−f,r_{\mathrm{eq}}=K(\widehat{\rho})\widehat{u}-f,

after applying boundary conditions, where K⁡(ρ^)K(\widehat{\rho}) is the stiffness matrix determined by the predicted density, u^\widehat{u} is the predicted displacement, and ff is the applied load. The volume residual rvolr_{\mathrm{vol}} measures deviation from the material budget. Compliance CC measures structural flexibility under the load. We retain the released denoising weights wtw_{t} and Gaussian residual penalties ℓt\ell_{t}, including their diffusion-dependent variances, for all optimizers.

Training and tuning.

We use batches of 16, 100 diffusion timesteps, constant learning rates, gradient clipping at 1, and no weight decay. An exponential moving average (EMA) of the parameters uses decay 0.99 after the first 1,000 updates.

Only learning rates are tuned. Each method initially tests five rates for 10,000 updates, extending the grid when needed. Selection uses the EMA validation objective on 128 fixed examples with fixed noise (Figure E.16). Final runs use a budget of 100,000 gradient evaluations.

Momentum and λ\lambda remain fixed. Muon uses β1=0.95\beta_{1}=0.95 with Nesterov; Adam, SOAP, and SoftServe-Kron use β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9. Adam and SOAP use β2=0.999\beta_{2}=0.999. SoftServe-Kron uses λ=9\lambda=9 without Nesterov. Matrix methods use the same convolution-kernel partitions, with blocks of at most 256×256256\times 256, and Adam at learning rate 10−410^{-4} on the remaining parameters.

Evaluation.

We evaluate the training objective on 32 fixed examples with fixed noise using the current, unaveraged parameters. Validation uses the EMA parameters on 128 separate fixed examples. Figure E.17 shows both objectives against gradient evaluations, parameter updates, and wall-clock time. All curves stop at 100,000 gradient evaluations. Including secant replay, this permits approximately 90,900 parameter updates for SoftServe-Kron and 100,000 for the baselines.

E.7 Language model

Task and data.

We train a language model on 200M tokens from FineWeb (Penedo et al., 2024). The task is to predict each token from its preceding context.

Model and objective.

We use a 16.17M-parameter GPT-style model (Radford et al., 2019) with four layers, four attention heads, hidden width 256, and context length 512. We minimize next-token cross-entropy, reported as negative log-likelihood (NLL) per token.

Training and tuning.

Each update uses 64 sequences, giving 32,768 tokens per full update. The 200M-token budget requires 6,104 updates, with a smaller final batch. Kron additionally uses 610 same-batch gradient replays. The learning rate warms up over the first 2% of training, remains constant, then decays by cosine to one tenth of its peak over the final 10%. We use no dropout, weight decay, or gradient clipping.

We tune learning rates on seed 0 using five-point sweeps at the full 200M-token budget, selecting by validation NLL. We first tune AdamW, then use its selected peak learning rate of 0.0030.003 for the AdamW updates outside the matrix methods. Muon, SOAP, and Kron update the same attention and MLP weight matrices, with AdamW on the remaining parameters. The selected peak learning rates are 0.0030.003 for Muon and SOAP, and 0.010.01 for Kron.

Kron uses λ=99\lambda=99, β1=0.99\beta_{1}=0.99, K=10K=10, and no Nesterov. Muon uses β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9 with Nesterov. SOAP uses betas (0.95,0.95)(0.95,0.95) and refreshes its preconditioner every 10 updates. AdamW uses betas (0.9,0.95)(0.9,0.95), both as a baseline and for the remaining parameters of the matrix methods. Momentum, Nesterov, and λ\lambda are fixed throughout tuning.

Evaluation.

We evaluate the selected configurations on fresh seeds 1–3 and report their mean NLL. Final training NLL uses one million training tokens; learning-rate selection and final validation NLL use five million held-out tokens.

Appendix F Ablation studies

We study the secant penalty λ\lambda, the accuracy of the Gram QME solver, and the refresh interval KK for SoftServe-Kron. Training studies use RNN Adding and minibatch MNIST, with budgets of 40,000 and 6,000 gradient evaluations, respectively, including secant replay. For each setting, we select the learning rate on seed 0 and evaluate on fresh seeds 1–3. RNN selection uses validation MSE; MNIST selection uses the mean of the last five training objectives. Test errors are not used for selection. Matching completed runs are reused.

Unless varied, λ=999\lambda=999, K=10K=10, and the solver uses 18 coupled root iterations and 10 inverse iterations. RNN uses β1=0.99\beta_{1}=0.99 and MNIST uses β1=0.95\beta_{1}=0.95, both with Nesterov momentum. Lines and points show arithmetic means; bands and error bars span the minimum and maximum over the three seeds.

F.1 Sensitivity to the secant penalty

We vary λ\lambda from 0.01 to 9999 on RNN Adding, retuning the learning rate for each value. Figure F.1 shows lower mean validation error as λ\lambda increases from 0.01 to 999. Values from 0.1 to 999 outperform the tuned Muon baseline in this experiment. Increasing λ\lambda further to 9999 causes numerical failure on all three evaluation seeds. Thus, the penalty can substantially affect both accuracy and stability; the best value here is not a task-independent default.

F.2 Accuracy of the QME solver

We first isolate numerical accuracy by solving 𝑸​𝑼​𝑸+𝑸=𝑽\bm{Q}\bm{U}\bm{Q}+\bm{Q}=\bm{V} for fixed 256×256256\times 256 matrices. We construct 𝑼=𝑹​𝑹⊤\bm{U}=\bm{R}\bm{R}^{\top} with singular values of 𝑹\bm{R} between 0.7 and 1.3, and use independent random eigenbases for 𝑼\bm{U} and 𝑽\bm{V}. The eigenvalues of 𝑽\bm{V} are logarithmically spaced from 1 to κ∈{10,103,105}\kappa\in\{10,10^{3},10^{5}\}. We vary both iteration counts in the FP32 Gram solver and compare with the FP64 decomposition-based solution 𝑸⋆\bm{Q}_{\star} using relative Frobenius error ‖𝑸^−𝑸⋆‖F/‖𝑸⋆‖F\|\widehat{\bm{Q}}-\bm{Q}_{\star}\|_{\mathrm{F}}/\|\bm{Q}_{\star}\|_{\mathrm{F}}.

Figure F.2 shows that too few iterations can leave substantial error. At the default 18/10 counts, median errors are approximately 2.3×10−62.3\times 10^{-6}, 7.3×10−57.3\times 10^{-5}, and 7.2×10−37.2\times 10^{-3} for the three values of κ\kappa. More iterations do not uniformly reduce FP32 error, particularly once rounding error limits accuracy.

We then vary the solver counts during RNN training (Figure F.3). We compare 12, 18, and 24 root iterations at 10 inverse iterations, and 10, 16, and 24 inverse iterations at 18 root iterations. Separate sweeps select a learning rate of 1.33×10−31.33\times 10^{-3} for all four stable settings. Their learning curves are similar; increasing either count beyond 18/10 does not consistently improve validation error. With 12/10, all three tested seed-0 learning rates fail before the full budget, so no fresh-seed mean is shown.

F.3 Refresh frequency and training cost

We compare K∈{1,5,10,20,50}K\in\{1,5,10,20,50\}, retuning the learning rate at each interval. Figure F.4 shows learning curves against gradient evaluations and wall-clock time. More frequent refreshes require more secant replays and leave fewer parameter updates within the same budget. Refreshing at every update slows convergence on both tasks. The best trade-off is task-dependent: K=5K=5 reaches the lowest mean RNN validation MSE, while larger intervals shorten MNIST training with similar final objectives.
